section_summary: This section documents U.S. State Department inquiries into Japanese dismissal and retirement allowances, beginning with a 1933 consular study of industrial practice and a detailed newspaper survey. A 1934–1935 correspondence with Chicago attorneys examines the customary allowance owed to a long-serving Japanese commercial employee, with the Tokyo consulate reporting that major firms commonly paid allowances based on final salary and years of service. The section concludes with a 1936 embassy despatch and full translation of Japan's Law No. 42, which required qualifying factories and mines to establish retirement reserves and allowances.

subfiles.title: Dismissal Allowances as a Feature of Japanese Labor Conditions, Report No. 117
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, American Consulate General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports on Japanese dismissal allowances, their legal basis, their relationship to retirement benefits, and their role in labor disputes.
subfiles.summary: The report explains that Japanese employment relations retained paternalistic features and that dismissal payments had historically been negotiated privately or paid voluntarily. The Revised Factory Act of 1926 required two weeks’ notice or two weeks’ pay for covered factory workers, while larger employers often paid more under pressure from labor or pursuant to collective arrangements. It also supplies 1931 labor-dispute statistics and emphasizes the difficulty that these practices created when estimating Japanese production costs.

subfiles.title: Only Big Concerns Paying Allowances
subfiles.to: Enclosed with Report No. 117 for the U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Surveys Japanese dismissal-allowance law, employer practices, collective agreements, and payment scales.
subfiles.summary: Article on a Tokyo Chamber survey: the Factory Law sets a minimum; large concerns commonly pay allowances while small employers pay only the minimum; dismissal and retirement allowances are often blurred.
keywords: Tokyo Chamber of Commerce and Industry

subfiles.title: Inquiry concerning a Japanese employee's retiring allowance
subfiles.from: Leland K. Neeves, Scott, MacLeish & Falk
subfiles.about: Requests information about the customary retirement allowance potentially owed to a Japanese employee with approximately twenty-five years of service.
subfiles.summary: Neeves says a client may close its Japanese branches and dismiss a long-serving employee paid 650 yen monthly who claims 40,000-50,000 yen by custom; he asks about the custom and calculation.

subfiles.title: Department of State communications and records routing notes
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.about: Records the internal routing of the July 1934 inquiry about Japanese retirement allowances.
subfiles.summary: These sparsely annotated pages contain Department of State communications and records markings associated with the Neeves inquiry. A handwritten date of August 3, 1934, and routing notations indicate internal handling rather than a substantive response.

subfiles.title: Request for further facts about the Japanese employee
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that the Department needs additional facts before asking the American Consul General at Tokyo to investigate the retirement-allowance question.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says the available information is inconclusive, the inquiry goes to Tokyo, and asks whether the employee was hired in Japan or the US and his duties.

subfiles.title: Draft reply on Japanese retiring allowances
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Offers a provisional explanation of Japanese law and custom governing retirement and dismissal allowances.
subfiles.summary: Draft reply: industrial workers have statutory protection, office staff customary treatment; the Factory Act's two-week minimum, scales, and a 1930 executive award; no uniform rule, so consult representatives in Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Castle despatch No. 22
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to Ambassador Castle's February 8, 1930 despatch concerning a retirement allowance.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Castle despatch 22 of February 8, 1930 on a retirement allowance.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the Department's August 2 letter
subfiles.from: Leland K. Neeves, Scott, MacLeish & Falk
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the proposed referral to Tokyo and promises additional information about the employee.
subfiles.summary: Neeves acknowledges the August 2 letter, notes referral to the Tokyo Consul General, and will provide facts after consulting his client.

subfiles.title: Further information on the employee's work history and compensation
subfiles.from: Leland K. Neeves, Scott, MacLeish & Falk
subfiles.about: Describes the Japanese employee's hiring, duties, salary, purchasing authority, and bonus arrangement.
subfiles.summary: Neeves says the employee began in New York in 1906, went to Japan in 1913 as purchasing commissionnaire, managed warehouses with funds around $50,000, earned 650 yen monthly and an incentive bonus of about $4,500.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment and notice of referral to Tokyo
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the attorney's follow-up information and confirms that the retirement-allowance inquiry has been sent to the American Consul General at Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Department acknowledges Neeves's follow-up, lacks enough information, and has referred the matter to Tokyo for a formal report.

subfiles.title: Instruction to prepare a report on Japanese retirement allowances
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Directs the Tokyo consulate to investigate Japanese retirement-allowance customs, legal rights, and calculation methods.
subfiles.summary: Instruction sends the consul general Neeves's letters and asks a report on custom, legal entitlement and calculation of retirement allowances.

subfiles.title: Payment of Retirement Allowances in Japan
subfiles.from: J. Holbrook Chapman, American Consul, American Consulate General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the retirement-allowance practices of major Japanese firms for administrative and executive personnel.
subfiles.summary: Chapman: schedules at Mitsui Bussan and the Yokohama Specie Bank run from 30 months' salary after ten years to 150 after thirty, 135 for twenty-five years; not compulsory but universal among large firms; comparable employees earned only 300-400 yen.

subfiles.title: Departmental reply on Japanese dismissal and retirement allowances
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Conveys the Tokyo consulate's findings about statutory dismissal pay and customary retirement allowances at large Japanese companies.
subfiles.summary: Department reply: the 1926 Factory Law gives covered workers two weeks' notice or wages, large employers pay more, executive allowances are customary, 135 months' pay after twenty-five years in two firms, with a caution on salaries.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of retirement-allowance information
subfiles.from: Leland K. Neeves, Scott, MacLeish & Falk
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State, attention Maxwell M. Hamilton
subfiles.about: Thanks the Department for information that precisely answered the firm's retirement-allowance inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Neeves thanks the Department for its January 26 reply and says the information is exactly what he wanted.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo despatch No. 2024
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japan's new statute requiring qualifying employers to establish retirement reserves and allowances.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Despatch 2024 translates the retirement-reserve law, covering businesses with fifty or more workers and requiring a two percent wage reserve.

subfiles.title: Law Providing for the Establishment of Retirement Reserves and Retirement Allowances by Employers for Their Employees, Despatch No. 2024
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits and explains a translation of Japan's Law No. 42 on compulsory retirement reserves and allowances.
subfiles.summary: Neville: Law 42 of June 2, 1936 requires factories and mines with fifty or more workers to reserve two percent of wages and protects against employer bankruptcy; born of post-February 26 reform demands, criticized for excluding small firms.

subfiles.title: A Law Providing for Retirement Reserves and Retirement Allowances, Law No. 42
subfiles.to: Enclosed with American Embassy despatch No. 2024 to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides the full English translation of Japan's 1936 statute regulating retirement reserves and allowances in qualifying factories and mining enterprises.
subfiles.summary: The law applies principally to factories and mining enterprises continuously employing at least fifty workers, while excluding certain short-term, day, and seasonal laborers until specified service thresholds are met. It requires employee retirement reserves and employer-funded retirement-allowance reserves generally calculated at two percent of wages, regulates investment and safeguarding of the funds, and establishes payment rules upon retirement, death, or dismissal. Special allowances are prescribed for workers dismissed for the employer’s convenience, and disputes must first go before a retirement money investigation committee. The statute also establishes inspection powers, penalties, transitional provisions, and amendments concerning taxation and postal-savings deposits.
